title: New Federal Data Shows How U.S. Public School Students Are Doing
summary:
A large federal survey called the Civil Rights Data Collection gives one of the most complete pictures of how students are treated in America's public schools. The newest report covers the 2023-24 school year and about 49.7 million students in more than 97,000 schools.

The government has gathered this kind of information for over 50 years. It helps the U.S. Education Department check whether schools protect students' civil rights. The Trump administration released the latest data on Aug. 31, six months later than promised.

Two researchers, Maithreyi Gopalan of the University of Oregon and Dan Losen of the National Center for Youth Law, studied the data and shared findings with NPR.

Preschool grew. About 1.5 million children were in public preschool, a 12% jump from 2021-22. Gopalan said some states are investing more in early learning. At the same time, K-12 enrollment fell almost 1%.

Suspensions rose. About 2.5 million students received out-of-school suspensions, up by about 100,000. Losen said students missed over 14 million school days because of them. He said many suspensions are for minor problems, such as being late, and that support for students and better teacher training can work better. The data also show Black students lost far more school days to suspension than white students.

Students with disabilities now make up 19% of public school students, up from 17%.

For the first time since the 1970s, the survey counted teachers by race. Teachers are 75% white, 9% Black and 11% Latino, very different from the students they teach.

The administration chose not to release data it collected on nonbinary students, citing an executive order. Losen criticized that choice. The Education Department did not answer NPR's questions about it.
why_it_matters: The survey is one of the main ways the country checks whether public schools treat all students fairly. Its findings on suspensions, preschool and teachers can shape how schools and lawmakers try to help students.

background_read: The Civil Rights Data Collection is a federal survey that asks public schools across the country to report information about their students and staff.
Civil rights laws say schools must treat students fairly no matter their race, sex or disability.
The U.S. Education Department uses the survey to check whether schools are following those laws and to spot groups of students who may be treated unequally.
Researchers and the public also study the results to see how things like preschool, discipline and teacher qualifications are changing.
